1.title: Know the words and the kinds of space to rent
1.intro: Renting out space means letting someone use part of your home or property for a fee. Start with the basics.
pts: Learn the terms: tenant, landlord, lease, deposit, short-term stay, long-term rental, occupancy, house rules.
Kinds of space you could rent out include a spare room, a basement suite, a parking spot or a storage area.
Name your guest or tenant in one line: who, how long, what they need.
Look at ten similar listings nearby and note price, rules and photos.
Compare long-term and short-term rental on income, work and risk.
Find the typical rent for a similar space and note the range.
List what a tenant expects: privacy, quiet, a lock and clear rules.
1.ex: A spare room near a college: tenants are students for eight months, need a quiet place, internet and a lease. If similar rooms rent for 650, 700 and 750, the middle price is 700.
1.act: Compare ten listings in a table and write a tenant profile.
1.std: Task: study ten listings. Condition: public pages. Standard: table complete and profile fits one line.

2.title: Explain how a rental runs from enquiry to move-out
2.intro: A rental has steps. If you can name them, you avoid conflict and loss.
pts: The steps: enquiry, viewing, check, agreement, move-in check, rent, repairs, notice, move-out check.
Complete a written move-in and move-out condition list with photos.
Agree who pays utilities, internet and repairs.
Keep every message and receipt in one folder.
Write the questions you ask at a viewing and the answers you need.
Plan the steps for ending a tenancy; check the provincial rule on notice.
Keep a key log: who has copies and when they were returned.
2.ex: At move-in you and the tenant walk through, photograph each room and both sign a condition list. At move-out you compare the same list. Any difference is discussed in writing.
2.act: Draw the steps for your space and write a move-in checklist.
2.std: Task: write a process and checklist. Condition: one page each. Standard: each step has an owner and a record.

3.title: Prepare and advertise the space honestly
3.intro: Now you apply the basics. Prepare a safe space and write an honest advertisement.
pts: Check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locks, wiring, exits and heat.
Take true photos and describe size, location, what is included and rules.
State rent, deposit if allowed, and length of stay.
Do not hide faults or use claims you cannot prove.
Press the test button on every alarm and write down the date you tested it.
Describe noise, shared spaces and parking in the ad.
State what the rent includes, such as heat, water and internet.
3.ex: Before: 'Cozy room, great location.' After: 'Furnished 12 m2 room, 10 minutes by bus to campus, internet included, no smoking.' If the room is 3 m by 4 m, 3 x 4 = 12 m2, so the size claim is true.
3.act: Prepare a room and write an advertisement with eight photos.
3.std: Task: prepare and advertise a space. Condition: with a safety checklist. Standard: alarms and exits checked, ad is true and complete.

4.title: Follow Canadian and local rules
4.intro: Housing law is mostly provincial and local rules also apply. Learn which ones touch you.
pts: Landlord and tenant law is set by each province: leases, deposits, rent increases, notice and entry rules differ. Check the current rule with the provincial tenancy office.
Short-term rental rules are set by cities and can need a licence or limit stays; check the current rule with the local authority.
Human rights law bars discrimination when choosing tenants.
Check insurance, mortgage and condo or co-op rules before you rent a space.
Ask the provincial tenancy office whether a deposit is allowed and how it must be held.
Find out how much notice a rent increase needs; check the provincial rule.
Keep a copy of every rule page you rely on, with the date.
4.ex: A city requires a licence for stays under a set number of days. You check the city page before you list and keep a copy. If the page says a licence number must appear in the ad, you add it.
4.act: Make a table of rule, who sets it, what you must do and where you checked, for ten items.
4.std: Task: build a rules table. Condition: from official public pages. Standard: each row has a dated source; unknowns say 'check the current rule with the local authority'.

5.title: Price the rent and check it pays
5.intro: Rent must cover costs and your time. Work the numbers.
pts: Costs: utilities, insurance, cleaning, repairs, supplies, platform fees, vacancy.
Vacancy is time with no renter; plan for some.
Net income = rent received minus costs.
Rental income is taxable in Canada; keep records and check the rules with the tax agency.
Build a table of twelve months with rent in and costs out.
Find the break-even rent: yearly costs divided by months rented.
Set aside part of the income for repairs.
5.ex: Rent is 700 a month, costs 180 a month, and one month a year is empty. Rent received = 700 x 11 = 7,700 and costs = 180 x 12 = 2,160, so yearly net = 7,700 - 2,160 = 5,540. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Build a one-page yearly budget with vacancy.
5.std: Task: compute yearly net income. Condition: with a spreadsheet. Standard: all costs listed and a mentor can follow the numbers.

6.title: Find good renters and set clear terms
6.intro: A good agreement protects both sides. Learn how to choose and to write terms.
pts: Ask the same questions of everyone and keep notes.
Check references and ask for proof of income where the law allows.
Write a lease or agreement with rent, term, rules, repairs and notice.
Give a copy to the renter and keep one.
Write house rules: noise, guests, smoking, cleaning and shared spaces.
Meet the applicant in person or by video before you decide.
Explain your decision in writing, using only your stated criteria.
6.ex: You ask each applicant: move-in date, length of stay, number of people, references. You use the same questions for all. You score each answer from 1 to 3, so the top total is 4 x 3 = 12, and you compare totals.
6.act: Write a one-page application form and a draft agreement; have a mentor review.
6.std: Task: draft the documents. Condition: using your province's public forms as a guide. Standard: terms are clear and no rule is guessed.

7.title: Protect safety, privacy and property
7.intro: Care for people, their information and the property is part of the job.
pts: Give the renter notice before entering, as the law requires.
Keep personal documents locked or password-protected.
Handle repairs quickly; urgent ones such as heat or water first.
Keep a log of repairs, cleaning and complaints.
Store spare keys safely and record who can use them.
Check that bedroom and entrance doors lock.
Take photos before and after repairs.
7.ex: A tap leaks on Friday night. You send a plumber that day, log it and tell the tenant what happened. If the call costs 120, you record 120 in the repairs column, and that month's net is 700 - 120 = 580 before other costs.
7.act: Write a repair log, a house rules page and an emergency list.
7.std: Task: write three documents. Condition: reviewed by a mentor. Standard: each is clear and dated.

8.title: Run a real pilot and decide
8.intro: Now you run it for real. Rent, measure and decide how to grow.
pts: Set a 60-day goal, such as one signed agreement and zero safety issues.
Every week record enquiries, costs, repairs and messages.
Ask the renter for feedback.
At the end choose: stop, change or grow, and write a 12-month plan.
Check your costs against the plan each month.
Write what you would change in the lease before the next renter.
Decide whether to continue, pause or stop and give reasons.
8.ex: After 60 days: 9 enquiries, 1 renter, 2 repairs fixed in 24 hours. 1 / 9 is about 11 percent of enquiries that became a renter. You decide to keep the rent and add a cleaning schedule.
8.act: Run the pilot, keep the weekly log and present a 12-month plan to a panel of three.
8.std: Task: run a 60-day pilot. Condition: real space, legal and with agreement. Standard: log complete, decision uses numbers, a panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is a lease?
A written agreement on rent, term and rules.
Who sets landlord and tenant law in Canada?
Mostly each province.
Why do a move-in condition list?
To show the state of the space and avoid disputes.
What safety items do you check?
Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, locks, wiring, exits and heat.
What is vacancy?
Time when no one is renting and no rent comes in.
Is rental income taxable?
Yes; keep records and check the rules with the tax agency.
Can you choose a tenant on any reason?
No; human rights law bars discrimination.
What do you do before entering a rented space?
Give notice as the law requires.
What do you check for short-term stays?
City licence and limits; check the current rule with the local authority.
What do you do when unsure about a rule?
Check the current rule with the local authority and keep the answer in writing.
